# About this guide {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-important title="Draft for feedback"}
This is a draft (October 2026). The chapter introductions and reading
lists are open for comments from the teachers. In particular: are
important papers missing, are any of them outdated, and is the level
right? The *Online lectures* sections have not been filled in yet.
:::

This book collects reading material for **Stora Tentan**, the 15 hp oral
exam in bioinformatics for PhD students at the Department of Biochemistry
and Biophysics (DBB), Stockholm University. It is built on the current exam
description (2025) and on the more detailed reading lists that were used in
earlier years.

## What the exam is

Stora Tentan should show that a student awarded a PhD from DBB has a good
basic knowledge of bioinformatics, *wider than their own thesis area*. The
exam assumes the knowledge needed to pass the department's advanced-level
courses in bioinformatics and comparative genomics, but it is primarily a
test of the ability to explain how bioinformatics methods are used to answer
fundamental biological questions. Students are also expected to follow
seminars and dissertations at DBB and SciLifeLab and to be aware of current
international research.

- Two examiners, about two hours.
- No single required textbook. Zvelebil & Baum [@zvelebil2008] or Pevsner
  [@pevsner2015] cover most areas, but they are not up to date — you need to
  update your knowledge to the current state of the art (the proceedings of
  the last few ISMB and ECCB meetings are a good start).
- The exam is **not** about knowing every detail. You should be able to
  discuss and reason about methods: how they work (algorithms), their
  advantages and limitations, and when to use them.
- Fundamental knowledge of the algorithms and limitations of established
  methods for **sequence searching, protein structure prediction, phylogeny
  and function annotation** is required.
- Every exam is unique. Depending on how the first topic goes, other topics
  may be covered in more or less depth, or not at all.

Experience shows that discussing the exam with other PhD students is a very
efficient way to prepare, and that online lectures often explain things
better than textbooks.

## How each chapter is organised

Each of the twelve topic chapters follows the same structure:

1. **Introduction** — a short overview of the topic.
2. **Key concepts** — a checklist of things you should be able to explain.
3. **Background reading** — open-access overviews (mostly Wikipedia and
   tutorials) to get started.
4. **Key papers** — reviews first, then classic papers and recent
   developments. Papers marked ★ were *mandatory* in earlier reading lists
   and are a good indication of the expected level.
5. **Online lectures** — recorded lectures that explain the topic well.

Full references are collected in [References](references.qmd); hover over a
citation to see it.

## Topics

| Topic | What is covered |
|---|---|
| [Sequence searching](chapters/01-sequence-searching.qmd) | Alignment algorithms, substitution matrices, BLAST, profile HMMs, significance, MSA, motifs |
| [Databases](chapters/02-databases.qmd) | Primary and derived databases, their hierarchy and relations |
| [Evolution](chapters/03-evolution.qmd) | Homology, orthology/paralogy, gene duplication, selection, drift |
| [Phylogeny](chapters/04-phylogeny.qmd) | Distance, parsimony, likelihood and Bayesian methods; models; support |
| [Genomics](chapters/05-genomics.qmd) | Sequencing technologies, assembly, read mapping, variant calling, gene prediction |
| [Genomes](chapters/06-genomes.qmd) | Prokaryotic vs. eukaryotic genome organisation, genome size and complexity |
| [Expression analysis](chapters/07-expression.qmd) | Microarrays, RNA-seq, single-cell, normalisation, multiple testing |
| [Proteomics](chapters/08-proteomics.qmd) | Mass spectrometry, peptide identification, quantification, FDR |
| [Protein structure](chapters/09-protein-structure.qmd) | Structure, domains, secondary/tertiary prediction, AlphaFold, design, docking |
| [Protein function](chapters/10-protein-function.qmd) | Function definitions (GO), annotation transfer, localisation, variant effects |
| [Protein–protein interactions](chapters/11-protein-interactions.qmd) | Experimental and computational PPI methods, networks |
| [Machine learning](chapters/12-machine-learning.qmd) | HMMs, neural networks, evaluation and overfitting, deep learning, language models |

## Earlier versions of the instructions

The reading lists from earlier years (in `data/`) contained a list of
mandatory articles and a much longer list of background papers. These have
been distributed over the topic chapters. A 2021 variant of the exam was
instead based on Pevsner's textbook [@pevsner2015] together with the review
by @sapoval2022; both remain excellent starting points.
